summary: This standards-track document defines the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) for NETCONF and RESTCONF. It provides a standard way to control which users may read, change or run operations on configuration data. The goal is secure, multi-vendor interoperable management that people can use easily.

eli5.summary: In a school, only some people may open the supply closet. This is a standard list of who may look at or change what on a network device.

questions: how does netconf access control work
what are the nacm crudx access rights
how does restconf map to nacm
subtitle: The standard permission system for NETCONF and RESTCONF: who may read, change or run what on a managed device.

tldr.problem: NETCONF and RESTCONF have no standard way to restrict which protocol operations and which content each user may access, so interoperable, controlled access was not possible.
tldr.mechanism: NACM groups users, applies ordered permit or deny rules per group for modules, operations, data nodes and notifications using a small create, read, update, delete, execute permission set, and falls back to global defaults when no rule matches.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 6536, adds RESTCONF support and covers the YANG 1.1 action and notification statements.

today: RFC 8341 is an Internet Standard (STD 91) and obsoletes RFC 6536; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What NACM Is For
sections.content:
The Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF, RFC 6241) and RESTCONF (RFC 8040) provide no standard mechanism to restrict the protocol operations and content that each user may access. RFC 8341 defines the NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM) to fill that gap, covering the Operations and Content layers of both protocols.

The RFC has three main parts: design objectives, the model itself, and a YANG data model (ietf-netconf-acm.yang). It obsoletes RFC 6536. The update adds RESTCONF support and handles two constructs new in YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950): the action statement, which is like rpc but sits inside a data node, and notification statements inside data nodes. These allow finer control than top-level rpc and notification statements.

It also clarifies that data node path matches include descendant nodes, and that write access is not required for data nodes changed implicitly by side effects, such as a YANG when expression changing result.
sections.eli5: Network devices can be changed remotely, but there was no shared rulebook for who is allowed to do what. NACM is that rulebook.

sections.title: Design Objectives
sections.content:
Because servers can add custom protocol operations, a model cannot just list the standard ones. NACM therefore protects three conceptual control points: protocol operation (may this operation be invoked), datastore (may these data nodes be read or altered) and notification (may this event type be received).

The other goals are simplicity (a small, familiar set of permissions and one rule set for operations, data and notifications), rules for single users or configurable groups, optional delegation of user-to-group mapping to a central server such as RADIUS, the ability to disable enforcement without deleting rules, and a standard YANG data model for configuring it.

The RFC also wants security-sensitive content to be identified in machine-readable form. Relying on documentation alone leaves a window of vulnerability after a new data model is loaded and before rules are configured, so a model designer should be able to tag content to be protected by default.
sections.eli5: The rules have to guard three doors: running commands, looking at or changing settings, and getting news alerts. They should also be easy enough that people actually use them.

sections.title: Where Checks Happen
sections.content:
Access control is applied to each <rpc> message except <close-session>, unless the session is a recovery session. The server first checks the user may invoke the protocol operation, then checks each data node the operation touches. For an action, read access is needed for every node in the hierarchy leading to it and execute access for the action node itself. For example, to use /interfaces/interface/reset-interface a group must be able to read /interfaces and /interfaces/interface and execute the action.

For notifications, the server checks read access to the notification and, for one inside a data subtree, to its ancestor nodes. A notification the user may not read is dropped for that subscription.

The model has features such as independent control of RPC, action, data and notification access, YANG security tags like nacm:default-deny-write, separate read, write and execute defaults, and counters of denied requests that the client can monitor.
sections.eli5: Think of guards at several doors. One checks whether you may ask for a job at all, another checks whether you may touch each thing the job needs, and another decides which news you may hear.

sections.title: Datastore Access and RESTCONF
sections.content:
The same rules apply to all datastores that support NACM. Conventional configuration datastores and the operational state datastore are controlled by NACM; local files, remote files and datastores accessed via the <url> parameter are not. Access is expressed with five rights, abbreviated CRUDX: create, read, update, delete and execute.

RESTCONF methods are mapped to NETCONF operations for access control. For example, a POST on a data resource is write access, but a POST on an operation resource is execute access. OPTIONS is not subject to NACM at all.

Some operations get special treatment. For <get> and <get-config>, nodes the client may not read are silently omitted along with their descendants, so filters keep working. <edit-config> is rejected with access-denied if it would create, delete or modify a node without the matching right. <delete-config> and <kill-session> are denied by default and the exec default does not apply to them. <discard-changes> only needs execute permission on the operation.
sections.eli5: Everyone gets up to five kinds of key: make something new, look, change, remove, or run. Web-style requests are translated into those same keys.

sections.title: Users, Groups, Switches and Rules
sections.content:
A user is a name derived from the transport layer when the session is established; if the transport cannot authenticate the user, the session is terminated. Access is granted to groups, not users: a group has a unique name and zero or more member usernames, and a user can belong to several groups. A server MAY support an emergency recovery session that bypasses all access control, which is useful for repairing a broken configuration. How it is identified is implementation specific.

Five global controls shape enforcement. enable-nacm turns enforcement on or off; when false, all requests are permitted. read-default, write-default and exec-default choose permit or deny when no rule matches. enable-external-groups decides whether group names reported by the transport layer are used.

There are four kinds of rule: module, protocol operation, data node and notification. Rules sit in ordered rule lists that apply to named groups.
sections.eli5: People are put into teams, and the rules are written for teams. There is also a master switch, some default answers for when no rule applies, and a spare key kept for emergencies.

sections.title: How a Request Is Decided
sections.content:
Rules are evaluated in a fixed order. The server MUST use the rules in effect when it starts processing a message for the whole message. Enforcement does not apply to server-initiated access such as loading the running configuration at boot, and if no access control configuration exists at first startup, the server MUST NOT allow any write access except to a recovery session.

For a protocol operation, the steps are: permit if enable-nacm is false, a recovery session, or <close-session>; otherwise find the user's groups (adding external groups if enabled); walk the rule lists in order and the rules inside each, and use the first matching rule's permit or deny. If nothing matches, nacm:default-deny-all denies, <kill-session> and <delete-config> are denied, and otherwise exec-default decides. Data node access follows the same pattern, where a path matches the node it names and its descendants, and falls back to nacm:default-deny-write, nacm:default-deny-all and the read and write defaults.

The server MUST NOT reveal information the client may not read in <error-info> or in restricted node contents in an <rpc-error>. A read that is denied simply leaves the data out of the reply.
sections.eli5: The guard checks the master switch, then reads the rule list top to bottom and obeys the first rule that fits. If none fits, the guard uses the default answer.

sections.title: The ietf-netconf-acm YANG Module
sections.content:
NACM is configured through a YANG module whose top container is /nacm. It holds the global switches, three read-only counters (denied-operations, denied-data-writes and denied-notifications), a groups list and an ordered rule-list list. Each rule has a name, a module-name, an optional rule type (protocol operation, notification or data node path), access-operations, an action of permit or deny, and an optional comment.

The module is the normative content that the server MUST support. Because the rule lists are ordered by the client, the server evaluates them in the order they appear in the running configuration datastore. The IANA section updates the registration of ietf-netconf-acm (prefix nacm) to reference RFC 8341 instead of RFC 6536.
sections.eli5: The rulebook is stored in a standard format, so any device and any management tool can read and edit it the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mandatory-to-implement secure transport for NETCONF is SSH and for RESTCONF is TLS. The RFC warns that responses to RESTCONF OPTIONS and PATCH must not vary with whether a resource exists, since that could be used to probe for values. Servers should return access-denied before exposing instance information.

Administrators are told to check the defaults: enable-nacm is true, read-default is permit, write-default is deny and exec-default is permit. They should restrict write and read access to the NACM data itself, make sure the mapping from transport identity to username is unique and correct, and consider setting enable-external-groups to false when the protocol that supplies group names, such as RADIUS, does not resist man-in-the-middle attacks.

Other risks include repeated edit attempts that reveal whether hidden data exists ("fishing"), non-standard operations with undocumented side effects, data that aliases sensitive data, leafref values that expose other nodes, and datastore locking used for denial of service. Data model designers should mark sensitive nodes with nacm:default-deny-write or nacm:default-deny-all.
sections.eli5: A rulebook is only as good as how it is set up. Check the default answers, protect the rulebook itself, and do not let sneaky guessing reveal what is hidden.

viz.caption: RESTCONF METHODS MAPPED TO ACCESS OPERATIONS (RFC 8341 TABLE 1)

items.label: all resources
items.desc: No NETCONF operation; no access operation, NACM not applied.

items.label: all resources
items.desc: Maps to get and get-config; read access.

items.label: operation
items.desc: Maps to the specified operation; execute access.

items.label: data
items.desc: Maps to edit-config; create and update access.

viz.caption: THE FOUR RULE TYPES IN NACM

items.title: Module rule
items.text: Controls access for definitions in a specific YANG module, identified by name.

items.title: Protocol operation rule
items.text: Controls a specific protocol operation, identified by its YANG module and name.

items.title: Data node rule
items.text: Controls a data node and its descendants, identified by path.

items.title: Notification rule
items.text: Controls a notification event type, identified by its YANG module and name.
